messages.content: What are the most common chords in a pop song?

function.name: music_theory_primary_triads
function.description: Get the primary triads for a given key signature. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

key_signature.description: The key signature to calculate the primary triads for.

include_inversions.description: Whether or not to include inversions in the returned triads.

message.content:
In most contemporary pop songs the harmonic palette is surprisingly small.  Musicians tend to rely on a handful of “core” chords that fit comfortably within the key and that sound fresh when repeated.  Below is a quick guide to the most common chords and progressions you’ll hear in pop music.

---

## 1. Primary Triads (I‑IV‑V)

These are the three diatonic chords built on the first, fourth, and fifth degrees of the scale.  They form the backbone of almost every pop progression.

| Key | I | IV | V |
|-----|---|----|---|
| C   | C | F  | G |
| G   | G | C  | D |
| D   | D | G  | A |
| A   | A | D  | E |

*If you want the inversions as well, just let me know the key and I can pull them up for you.*

---

## 2. The “Pop‑Song” Progression: I‑V‑vi‑IV

This four‑chord loop is arguably the most ubiquitous in pop.  It works in any key and gives a satisfying sense of resolution while still sounding modern.

| Key | I | V | vi | IV |
|-----|---|---|----|----|
| C   | C | G | Am | F  |
| G   | G | D | Em | C  |
| D   | D | A | Bm | G  |
| A   | A | E | F#m| D  |

> **Why it works**  
> • The vi chord (minor) adds emotional depth.  
> • The IV chord provides a lift before returning to the tonic.  
> • The progression can be looped endlessly without sounding repetitive.

---

## 3. Minor‑Key Counterparts

When a pop track is in a minor key, the same pattern often appears but with the relative major chords swapped:

| Key | i | v | VI | III |
|-----|---|---|----|-----|
| A♭m | A♭m | E♭ | C♭ | F♭ |

(Use the relative major’s I‑IV‑V instead of the minor’s i‑v‑VI.)

---

## 4. Secondary Dominants & Substitutions

To spice things up, pop writers sprinkle in secondary dominants (e.g., V/V, V/vi) or use the “Neapolitan” (♭II) or “Picardy third” (major V in a minor key).  These are optional but add color.

---

## 5. Common Chord Progressions (in any key)

| Progression | Description |
|-------------|-------------|
| I–V–vi–IV | Classic pop loop |
| ii–V–I | Jazz‑influenced turnaround |
| vi–IV–I–V | “50s progression” |
| I–vi–IV–V | “doo‑wop” style |
| I–IV–V–IV | Simple, upbeat feel |
| I–iii–IV–V | Adds a bright, hopeful tone |

---

### Quick Example in C Major

```
C   G   Am  F
I   V   vi  IV
```

Play each chord for one bar (or two if you want a slower feel), and you’ve got a full‑length pop chorus.

---

## Want the exact chord voicings?

If you’d like the actual chord shapes (including inversions) for a particular key, just tell me the key and whether you want inversions.  I can then call the `music_theory_primary_triads` function to fetch them for you.
